newsitem.title: USA: U.S. March budget gap narrows dramatically.
newsitem.headline: U.S. March budget gap narrows dramatically.

text.p: The gap between the government's income and its spending narrowed dramatically in March from a year earlier, the Treasury Department said Monday, aided by a healthy economy that fattened tax revenues.
The spending deficit last month was $21.32 billion, less than half the $47.07 billion posted in March 1996, the Treasury said. It followed a $44.01 billion shortfall in February.
Analysts said the big improvement during March should encourage lawmakers who are struggling to come up with a political compromise on competing visions about how to balance the budget by 2002.
On Sunday, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said in a television interview that he thought "the iron is hot" for an agreement with the Clinton administration on a balanced budget.

"I think we can come to an agreement," Lott said, though differences remain over White House efforts to limit cuts to programs like Medicare and over the Republican-controlled Congress' desire for tax cuts.
Total government spending declined during March to $129.42 billion from $134.3 billion in February and was down from $136.16 billion in March 1996.
But the big difference came on the revenue side.

Total revenues from taxes, fees and all other sources climbed to $108.1 billion in March from $90.29 billion in February. A year earlier in March 1996, the government took in $89.09 billion of revenues.

During the first six months of fiscal 1997 that ends on Sept. 30, the cumulative budget deficit dropped 13 percent to $111.28 billion from $127.71 billion in the comparable first six months of fiscal 1996.

Economist Kathleen Stephansen of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York said she hoped budget negotiators would keep the pressure on for a deal to ratchet down spending in order to get deficits under control.
"I hope that this won't bring about a degree of complacency," Stephansen said. "I think that policymakers should be encouraged but by no means should they call it a day.

"There needs to be permanent mechanisms put in place for controlling spending because a lot of this (improvement) is cyclical," she added. The economy began its seventh year of expansion in March, generating higher personal incomes from steady job growth and sturdy growth in corporate profits.

During March, receipts from individual tax payments eased down slightly to $36.43 billion from $37.4 billion in February. But corporate tax payments jumped to $18.72 billion last month from $2.24 billion in February.

Many corporations pay their taxes in quarterly instalments and March marked the end of the first quarter. Tax receipts from individuals will swell in April because of the mid-month deadline for filing 1996 returns.
The Clinton administration has forecast a deficit for all of fiscal 1997 of $125.59 billion, up from a deficit in fiscal 1996 of $106.99 billion, but many analysts think that estimate is too high.
Stephansen said that, after the March figures, she was revising down her estimated deficit for the full 1997 fiscal year to $100 billion from $110 billion.
